cross_tool_domains.attrition: Some concern (administrative missingness; participant attrition not applicable): There is no human-subject follow-up, but administrative indicator completeness is incomplete—sewage quality indicators IN082 and IN077 are entirely missing ('-' in Table 4, pp. 18-19) and water indicators INp001 and INp002 listed in Table 1 (p. 12) drop out of Table 3 (pp. 15-16).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern / Weak: Descriptive two-year single-municipality case study with no counterfactual or statistical control for demographic, hydrological, urban-settlement, or fiscal confounders; narrative comparisons to Brasiléia, Acre, the North region, and national averages (pp. 16-19) are unadjusted.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Adequate: Accurately identifies key federal water and sanitation statutes (Laws 9.433/1997, 11.107/2005, 11.445/2007, 14.026/2020), Rio Branco's institutional delegation trajectory (DOV, SAAE, SANACRE, DEPASA, SAERB), and normative regulatory standards (PLANSAB, Portaria MS 05/2017, ProEESA Reg 2, ACERTAR, Sunshine regulation), though ACERTAR confidence/accuracy audit scores are not formally operationalized and Table 2 has threshold transcription gaps.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: High concern / Weak: Relies on utility self-declared SNIS records audited by AGEAC during the first ACERTAR cycle, which Section 4.1 (p. 14) explicitly reports suffered from equipment imprecision, missing operational procedures, and compromised water-quality sample integrity; compounded by unit typos and non-exhaustive intervals in Table 2 (p. 13) and coding contradictions in Section 4.3 / Table 3 (pp. 15-16).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak: Although outcome definitions draw on standardized SNIS/Regulasan water and sewage indicators, raw numeric values for 2018 and 2019 are omitted for most indicators in Tables 3-4, sewage quality outcomes (IN082, IN077) lack data, underlying DEPASA metering/sampling accuracy was compromised, and Section 4.3 mislabels IN009 as Macromedição (94.79%) while coding 94.79% as Ideal despite a >=95% threshold.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: High concern / Weak: No pre-specified protocol; selective and inconsistent reporting between indicator selection and results (INp001 and INp002 disappear after Table 1; raw annual values are largely omitted in favor of categorical 'x' marks; table cross-references are misnumbered; prose and Table 3 contradict Table 2 thresholds).
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern / Weak: Purposive single-case selection of one municipal system (Rio Branco under DEPASA in 2018-2019) and non-systematic selection of 21 Regulasan/SNIS indicators based loosely on data availability (Section 3.5, p. 12), with 4 selected indicators omitted from the normative threshold matrix (Table 2) or evaluation tables.

domain_ratings.justification: Primary Brazilian water and sanitation laws and regulatory instruments are accurately cited by number and year—including Federal Law No. 9.433/1997, Laws No. 11.107/2005 and 11.445/2007, Law No. 14.026/2020 (New Legal Framework for Basic Sanitation), Ministry of Health Portaria MS 05/2017, and PLANSAB—alongside AGEAC and ARSESP regulatory frameworks. Rated adequate rather than strong because statutory analysis relies largely on secondary commentary (e.g., Resk, 2020) without article-level pinpoints, and several cited statutes/ordinances are omitted from the reference list.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 1, 3, 6, 12-13, 20-24 (Abstract; Section 1; Section 2.3; Section 3.6 Table 2; Section 5; References)

domain_ratings.justification: The study precisely bounds its geographic, administrative, and temporal jurisdiction to potable water and sanitation provision in the Municipality of Rio Branco, State of Acre (Baixo Acre development region), during base years 2018-2019 under state provider DEPASA, while clearly documenting the historical institutional transitions from DOV, SAAE (1969), and SANACRE (1971) to shared state-municipal delegation under DEPASA (2012) and subsequent municipal reversion to SAERB (2021).

The regulatory/institutional regime under evaluation—first-cycle ACERTAR regulatory auditing by the state regulator AGEAC combined with Sunshine regulation ('regulação por exposição') benchmarking against PLANSAB, Portaria MS 05/2017, and ProEESA Reg 2 reference bands—is conceptually clearly described. However, the formal ACERTAR confidence and accuracy grading criteria are not operationalized in detail.

Service performance outcomes are defined via 21 standardized SNIS / Projeto Regulasan indicators spanning access, efficiency, and quality for water and sewage (Table 1) and mapped onto three normative performance bands (Ideal, Satisfatório, Insatisfatório) in Table 2. Rated adequate rather than strong because 4 of the 21 indicators in Table 1 (INp002, INp001, IN082, IN077) have no threshold definitions in Table 2, and Table 2 introduces unit errors ('%' instead of l/dia/lig for IN051 and kWh/m³ for IN058) and non-contiguous numeric intervals (e.g., IN013 gap between 0% and >10%; IN015 gap between <20.96% and >=60.27%).

The empirical unit of analysis—the municipal water and sanitation system of Rio Branco (estimated population 419,452: 385,895 urban and 33,556 rural) operated by DEPASA across base years 2018 and 2019—is explicitly stated. However, the scope is restricted to aggregate municipal-year figures from the first ACERTAR cycle (with occasional ad hoc 2020/2021 SNIS citations in prose) without neighborhood-level disaggregation despite framing intra-municipal vulnerability as a core concern.

Indicator selection from the Regulasan/SNIS catalog is justified only broadly as choosing those that best represent services offered and available basic information (p. 12), without explicit inclusion/exclusion rules. Four indicators selected in Table 1 (INp001, INp002, IN082, IN077) are dropped from the threshold rubric (Table 2) or omitted/unmeasured in the final evaluation tables (Tables 3-4) without systematic explanation.

Data come from AGEAC's Relatório de Fiscalização and Relatório de Certificação auditing DEPASA's SNIS submissions. Raw numeric values for 2018 and 2019 are omitted for many indicators (Tables 3-4 show only categorical 'x' marks), Section 4.1 explicitly notes that DEPASA suffered from equipment imprecision and compromised water sample integrity affecting data accuracy, there is a magnitude typo on p. 5 ('15 milhões' vs '13,7 bilhões'), and Section 4.3 misidentifies IN009 as Índice de Macromedição (94.79%) whereas Table 1/2 define IN009 as Hidrometração and IN011 as Macromedição.

The study is a descriptive two-year single-municipality case study applying normative thresholds via simple descriptive statistics. It lacks any temporal pre-post intervention structure, control group, or identification strategy capable of isolating causal impacts of legal reforms, institutional transitions, or Sunshine/ACERTAR regulation on water and sewage outcomes.

No analytical or design-based adjustments are made for structural, demographic, hydrological, or fiscal confounders when interpreting Rio Branco's indicator performance or making brief narrative comparisons with Brasiléia, Acre state averages, the North region, and national SNIS averages.

The paper provides detailed institutional, historical, and operational context on Acre's rubber-cycle urban formation, Rio Branco's water infrastructure (ETA Sobral, deactivation of the polluted Igarapé Judia system, ETA II), successive utility governance shifts (DOV, SAAE, SANACRE, DEPASA, SAERB), AGEAC regulatory auditing, and principal-agent information asymmetry in self-reported SNIS data.

Primary audit documents (AGEAC Relatório de Fiscalização and Relatório de Certificação) were obtained by formal request rather than a public archive, raw 2018 and 2019 indicator scores are not comprehensively reported in Tables 3-4, and unit/interval inconsistencies in Table 2 prevent exact independent reproduction of all ratings.

Although Table 2 states traffic-light thresholds (Ideal, Satisfatório, Insatisfatório), categorical coding in Tables 3-4 cannot be audited for indicators lacking reported raw values and exhibits direct internal contradictions: p. 16 reports 94.79% for Macromedição (misattributed to IN009), which falls below Table 2's >=95% Ideal threshold for IN011 yet is coded Ideal in Table 3; Table 2 leaves numeric gaps for IN013 (between 0% and >10%) and IN015 (between <20.96% and >=60.27%); and Section 4.1's qualitative audit summary specifies no documentary coding protocol.

overall_narrative_summary: Martellet et al. (2024) present a single-municipality institutional and regulatory-empirical case study evaluating water supply and sanitation performance in Rio Branco, Acre, Brazil (2018-2019, under state provider DEPASA) using SNIS/Regulasan administrative indicators audited by state regulator AGEAC under the first ACERTAR cycle and classified via the Sunshine regulation traffic-light model. Appraised under the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework (structured non-validated judgment, no numeric composite score), the study demonstrates strong jurisdictional specificity and institutional contextualization—tracing Rio Branco's water/sanitation governance from DOV, SAAE, and SANACRE to DEPASA and SAERB alongside federal legal frameworks (Laws 9.433/1997, 11.445/2007, 14.026/2020)—and adequate framing of regulatory exposure and indicator domains. However, empirical and methodological rigor is weak overall due to non-systematic indicator selection and attrition across tables (INp001, INp002, IN082, IN077), severe underlying utility measurement defects noted in the audit itself (equipment inaccuracies and compromised sample integrity), omission of raw 2018-2019 values for many indicators, internal threshold and coding contradictions between Table 2, Table 3, and Section 4.3 (e.g., mislabeling IN009 vs IN011 and coding 94.79% as Ideal against a >=95% threshold), absence of causal identification or confounding control, limited replicability of non-public AGEAC audit files, and lack of researcher reflexivity.
overall_rating: Structured non-validated judgment: Weak methodological rigor overall (2 strong domains [jurisdictional specificity, institutional context], 3 adequate domains [legal source accuracy, exposure definition, outcome definition], and 8 weak domains [selection process, measurement transparency, causal identification, confounding, replication potential, coding transparency, researcher reflexivity], with adequate sampling transparency)
study_design_identified: Single-municipality institutional and regulatory-empirical case study (descriptive Sunshine regulation benchmarking of secondary SNIS/Regulasan administrative indicators and AGEAC first-cycle ACERTAR audit reports for Rio Branco, Acre, in 2018-2019)
where_found_summary: Abstract (PDF pp. 1-2); Section 1 Introduction (pp. 2-4); Section 2 Theoretical/Institutional Background (pp. 4-7); Section 3 Method, Study Area, Indicator Selection, and Sunshine Thresholds Tables 1-2 (pp. 8-14); Section 4 Results and Discussion, Tables 3-4 (pp. 14-19); Section 5 Final Considerations (pp. 19-21); References (pp. 21-24).
why_tool_chosen: Although Section 3.2 labels the paper 'descritivo, qualitativo e quantitativo', it conducts neither primary qualitative data collection/coding (interviews, focus groups, ethnography) nor sample-based quantitative survey/inferential analysis or quasi-experimental comparison. Instead, it is a single-jurisdiction doctrinal/regulatory-empirical institutional case study combining legal-historical analysis of water and sanitation governance in Rio Branco with administrative audit reports (ACERTAR) and normative threshold benchmarking (Sunshine regulation) of a single utility (DEPASA, 2018-2019). Per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §§1-2, single-case institutional/regulatory histories without a comparator arm or human-subject sample do not fit ROBINS-I, JBI Cross-Sectional, CASP, or MMAT, making the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework the exact matching instrument.
